---
title: "Error handling"
description: "Handle remote module loading failures gracefully using error boundaries and fallback strategies"
---

Remote modules can fail to load for reasons outside your control: the remote server is down, a network request times out, a version mismatch causes the remote container to reject initialization, or a CDN edge node serves a stale manifest. Unhandled failures produce blank screens or uncaught promise rejections that crash the entire host application.

The patterns in this section let you contain failures to the affected micro frontend and keep the rest of the application functional.

## Why remote modules fail

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Remote is offline">
    If the server serving `remoteEntry.js` is unreachable, the browser's `<script>` injection fails with a network error. The federation runtime throws an unhandled rejection unless you wrap the import.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Version mismatch">
    When `requiredVersion` is set and no loaded instance satisfies it, the runtime either logs a warning (default) or throws (when `strictVersion: true`). In singleton mode a mismatch can cause subtle bugs rather than an explicit error.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Remote container initialization failure">
    The remote's own bootstrap code may throw — for example, if it tries to access an API at startup that is unavailable. This surfaces as a rejected promise on the dynamic import.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Chunk loading errors">
    After the container is initialized, lazy loading individual exposed modules can still fail if the chunk file is missing or the CDN returns a non-200 response.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## The `error-boundary` example

This example demonstrates the full offline-remote failure scenario. Only `app1` is started; `app2` remains offline.

| App  | Port | State   |
| ---- | ---- | ------- |
| app1 | 3001 | Running |
| app2 | 3002 | Offline |

`app1` declares `app2` as a remote and lazily imports `app2/Button`. Because `app2` is offline, the import fails. A runtime plugin intercepts the failure and renders an error message as a React module in place of the missing component. The rest of the application continues to function normally.

### Configuration

`app1` uses `@module-federation/enhanced` with `asyncStartup: true`, which defers module execution to after federation has initialized — a prerequisite for plugins that need to intercept early lifecycle hooks.

<CodeGroup>

```js error-boundary/app1/webpack.config.js
const { ModuleFederationPlugin } = require('@module-federation/enhanced/webpack');
const deps = require('./package.json').dependencies;

new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  experiments: { asyncStartup: true },
  name: 'app1',
  filename: 'remoteEntry.js',
  remotes: {
    app2: 'app2@http://localhost:3002/remoteEntry.js',
  },
  exposes: {
    './Button': './src/Button',
  },
  shared: {
    ...deps,
    react: { singleton: true },
    'react-dom': { singleton: true },
  },
})
```

```js error-boundary/app1/rspack.config.js
const {
  HtmlRspackPlugin,
  container: { ModuleFederationPlugin },
} = require('@rspack/core');
const deps = require('./package.json').dependencies;

new ModuleFederationPlugin({
  experiments: { asyncStartup: true },
  name: 'app1',
  filename: 'remoteEntry.js',
  remotes: {
    app2: 'app2@http://localhost:3002/remoteEntry.js',
  },
  exposes: {
    './Button': './src/Button',
  },
  shared: {
    ...deps,
    react: { singleton: true },
    'react-dom': { singleton: true },
    lodash: {},
  },
})
```

</CodeGroup>

### React error boundary wrapping the remote import

`app1/src/App.js` wraps the lazy remote import in both `React.Suspense` (for the loading state) and a class-based `ErrorBoundary` (for the failure state). If `app2/Button` fails to load for any reason, `ErrorBoundary` catches it and renders a fallback message instead of crashing the page.

```jsx error-boundary/app1/src/App.js
import React from 'react';
import LocalButton from './Button';

const RemoteButtonLazy = React.lazy(() => import('app2/Button'));

const App = () => (
  <div>
    <h1>Offline Remote</h1>
    <h2>Remotes currently in use</h2>
    {__FEDERATION__.__INSTANCES__.map(inst => (
      <span key={inst.name}>{inst.name}</span>
    ))}
    <LocalButton />
    <ErrorBoundary>
      <React.Suspense fallback="Loading Button">
        <RemoteButtonLazy />
      </React.Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
    <button onClick={() => { localStorage.clear('button'); window.location.reload(); }}>
      Reset
    </button>
  </div>
);

class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component {
  state = { hasError: false };

  componentDidCatch(error, errorInfo) {
    console.error(error, errorInfo);
    this.setState({ hasError: true });
  }

  render() {
    const { children } = this.props;
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return (
        <div>
          <h1>Something went wrong</h1>
          <p>Try refreshing the page.</p>
        </div>
      );
    }
    return children;
  }
}
```

### Running the example

<Steps>
  <Step title="Start only app1">
    ```bash
    cd error-boundary/app1
    pnpm start
    ```
    Do **not** start `app2`. Leave port 3002 empty.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Open the host">
    Navigate to [http://localhost:3001](http://localhost:3001). The page loads and renders the local button. The area where `app2/Button` would appear shows the error boundary fallback instead.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Inspect the runtime">
    Open the browser console. You will see the network error for `http://localhost:3002/remoteEntry.js` and the error caught by `componentDidCatch`. The rest of the application is unaffected.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## React error boundaries with federated components

The pattern from the example generalizes to any federated component. Wrap every remote import in the same structure:

```jsx
import React from 'react';

const RemoteComponent = React.lazy(() => import('remote/Component'));

function SafeRemote() {
  return (
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Remote unavailable.</p>}>
      <React.Suspense fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}>
        <RemoteComponent />
      </React.Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  );
}
```

<Warning>
  `React.Suspense` alone does not catch errors — it only handles the loading state. You must combine it with an `ErrorBoundary` to handle load failures. A pending `React.lazy` that rejects will propagate to the nearest error boundary, not the nearest `Suspense` boundary.
</Warning>

## Retry and fallback patterns

### Promise-based remote with inline fallback

The `shared-routes2` example shows how to wrap the remote declaration itself in a `Promise` that resolves to a stub container when the remote is offline. This prevents the error from reaching React at all:

```js webpack.config.js
remotes: {
  app2: `promise new Promise(function (resolve, reject) {
    __webpack_require__.l(
      "http://localhost:3002/remoteEntry.js",
      function (event) {
        if (typeof app2 !== 'undefined') return resolve();
        reject(new Error('Loading script failed'));
      },
      "app2",
    );
  }).catch(function(e) {
    console.log('remote offline, using stub');
    return {
      get: (module, scope) => () => [],
      init: () => {},
    };
  })`,
},
```

The stub container returns an empty module list for every `get` call, so `React.lazy` receives an empty module and the Suspense fallback or error boundary handles the empty result.

### Runtime plugin fallback

For more control, implement a runtime plugin that intercepts `loadRemote` or container initialization failures and returns a synthetic module. The `offline-remote` example in `runtime-plugins/offline-remote` demonstrates this approach: the plugin catches the network failure and renders a React error message directly as the remote module, so consumers never see an exception.

## Self-healing for missing shared dependencies

A related failure mode is when a remote expects a shared dependency that the host did not provide. Module Federation handles this automatically through the self-healing mechanism: the runtime fetches the missing package from the remote's own bundle rather than failing.

See [Shared dependencies](/examples/shared-dependencies) for a full walkthrough of the `self-healing` example.

## Best practices

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Always wrap remote imports in Suspense + ErrorBoundary" icon="shield">
    Every `React.lazy(() => import('remote/X'))` call must be wrapped in both. Suspense handles the pending state; ErrorBoundary handles the rejected state. Neither alone is sufficient.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Provide meaningful fallback UI" icon="layout">
    The `fallback` prop on `Suspense` and the error render in `ErrorBoundary` should match the approximate size of the missing component to prevent layout shift. A skeleton or placeholder beats a blank space or an abrupt error message.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Log errors in componentDidCatch" icon="terminal">
    Call `console.error` or send to your error tracking service inside `componentDidCatch`. Silent swallowing makes diagnosing remote load failures in production very difficult.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Test with remotes offline" icon="wifi-slash">
    Regularly run your host application with one or more remotes intentionally stopped. This validates that your error boundaries behave correctly and that the rest of the application remains functional.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

<Tip>
  Use a shared `RemoteBoundary` wrapper component in your design system that combines `Suspense` and `ErrorBoundary` with consistent loading and error states. This prevents teams from forgetting one of the two and keeps the fallback UI consistent across all federated components.
</Tip>
